moves.speaker: Michael Shermer

moves.warrant: Shermer argues that when the full set of opportunities is counted, the law of large numbers predicts that unusual matches will sometimes occur.
moves.inference: Mere improbability does not establish divine intervention, so miracle claims require a stronger evidential standard.

moves.description: Shermer argues that rare coincidences become expected across enormous numbers of opportunities, so apparent improbability by itself does not justify inferring any miraculous intervention.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Shermer converts an intuitive coincidence into a frequency argument, emphasizing that enormous opportunity sets predict occasional astonishing outcomes without supernatural intervention and thereby directly challenges the inference from improbability to miracle. Principal limitation: The reasoning fits coincidences generated by many trials, but it does not establish that every reported healing, resurrection, or purposive event belongs to an adequately specified repeatable class with enough relevant opportunities. Live burden: Shermer must identify the comparison class and show that chance, misperception, or transmission plausibly explains the particular reports under dispute, while Vandeweghe still must demonstrate why those reports exceed ordinary probabilistic expectations.
